description: Foreigner-marker drills (ranked), the five-card tradition switch set, and same-word-two-traditions pairs. verified:false means the research notes list the claim as unverified or unsourced.

drills.title: Resh: back of the throat, not the English r
drills.marker: English [ɹ] ("rail") instead of the Israeli uvular [ʁ̞].
drills.listenFor: The tongue tip does nothing. The sound is made at the back of the mouth, like the r in French or German; HebrewPod101 compares it to gargling air at the back of your throat.
drills.tryThis: Say kar, rishon, horim, rekhev slowly, keeping the tongue tip down behind the lower teeth.

examples.note: gloss is lane-3; the word is HebrewPod101's

drills.title: Five pure, short vowels: no glides
drills.marker: Diphthongised English vowels (sha-LOHM with an "oh-oo" glide).
drills.listenFor: Each vowel is one steady, short sound: a e i o u. Native Hebrew has only two true diphthongs, /aj/ and /ej/, and vowel length does not change meaning.
drills.tryThis: Say lo, bo, lu, li, la with no trailing w or y sound; clip them.

examples.note: say the second vowel as a plain [o], not "oh-oo"

drills.note: The Talkpal page is a low-authority learner site; the Wikipedia phonology claim (five vowels, length not contrastive) carries the drill.

drills.title: Stress usually falls on the last syllable (milra)
drills.marker: English-habit stress on the first or second syllable.
drills.listenFor: Most Hebrew words are stressed on the final syllable: begadIM, yaldA, lilmOD. Real exceptions exist (SEfer, medabEret, tapUach).
drills.tryThis: Clap the syllables and land the clap on the last one.

unverifiedExtras.text: Stress minimal pairs bóker (morning) / bokér (cowboy) and yaldá (girl) / yálda (she gave birth) are lane-3 background knowledge, NOT from a fetched source. Confirm in a dictionary and with a native speaker before publishing.

drills.title: Silent shva makes consonant clusters
drills.marker: Inserting a short vowel in g-dola, k-tana, z-man.
drills.listenFor: Native speakers often say no vowel at all: gdola, ktana, zman. New speakers put a short vowel between the two consonants.
drills.tryThis: Say zman, then gdola, holding the two consonants together with no vowel between them.

examples.note: name list is HebrewPod101's: b'dihah; gloss lane-3

drills.note: For prayer reading the historical shva rules apply instead (see src/pronunciation/shva.js); this drill is for spoken Israeli Hebrew. No corpus measures how often Israelis drop shva na.

drills.title: Do not carry shul pharyngeals into Israeli speech
drills.marker: Pharyngeal chet and ayin (the strict synagogue sound).
drills.listenFor: Chet is the same sound as khaf (like the ch in Bach); ayin sounds like alef (a glottal stop or nothing). Only some older Mizrahi speakers keep the pharyngeals.
drills.tryThis: Say chet as a throat-clearing kh, and read ayin as if it were alef.

examples.note: ayin read as alef; gloss lane-3

unverifiedExtras.text: A [k] / [χ] / [h] contrast set (kar / char / har type triples) was suggested in the notes as "construct and verify". The set below is hand-built, not minimal, and not checked by a native speaker.

drills.title: Less puff on p, t, k
drills.listenFor: Hebrew p, t, k are commonly described as less aspirated than English. The fetched phonology page does NOT state this.
drills.tryThis: Hold a hand in front of your mouth and say pita, toda, kafe with as little breath as you can.
drills.unverifiedReason: Not sourced in the research notes (listed as a gap). Needs a phonetics reference or a native speaker.

switchCards.title: Kamatz: a becomes o
switchCards.rule: Where Israeli/Sephardi reads kamatz gadol as a, Ashkenazi reads it as o (aw). Patach stays a.

sources.label: Chabad: The Difference Between Sepharadic and Ashkenazic Pronunciation

switchCards.title: Cholam: o stays o, or becomes oy
switchCards.to: o (southern German, many US Ashkenazim) or oy (Polish/Chasidic)
switchCards.rule: Choose one value for your community. Most American Ashkenazi readers use o; oy is the Polish/Galician/Chasidic value.

examples.gloss: my Lord (the divine name is read this way)

sources.label: Chabad: The Difference Between Sepharadic and Ashkenazic Pronunciation

switchCards.note: The o/oy choice per community is documented only qualitatively; the spelling "Toyrah" is unsourced in our notes.

switchCards.title: Tzere: e becomes ei
switchCards.rule: Ashkenazi tzere is a diphthong. Segol stays e.

examples.note: same in both: the yod already spells ei

sources.label: Chabad: The Difference Between Sepharadic and Ashkenazic Pronunciation

switchCards.title: Tav without dagesh: t becomes s
switchCards.rule: Only tav WITHOUT a dagesh changes. A tav with dagesh is t in every tradition.

sources.label: Chabad: The Difference Between Sepharadic and Ashkenazic Pronunciation

switchCards.title: Stress: last syllable becomes second-to-last
switchCards.rule: Ashkenazi stress is historically penultimate (SHAB-bos, KID-dush). The sources do not say how consistently American prayer reading follows this; that part is inference.
switchCards.note: Penultimate stress in American prayer reading is lane-3 inference, not a sourced fact.

switchConsistency.text: If you change tradition, change all five switches together, including the divine name. All dialects of Hebrew are acceptable; consistency within the prayer is what matters.

sources.label: Chabad: The Difference Between Sepharadic and Ashkenazic Pronunciation

switchConsistency.sameInBoth: Aleph/ayin silent, chet=khaf and the resh are the same in General Israeli and common Ashkenazi practice (per the notes), so they are not switches.
